chunks: Floorplanning subsystems on a PCB. The question: How do you decide which subsystems go where on a PCB?
Floorplanning means deciding where each functional block goes on the board before drawing any traces.
You group circuits by job, separate the noisy ones from the sensitive ones, put each power supply near the part it feeds, and keep connectors where the enclosure needs them.
Clever routing cannot fix a bad floorplan.
Think of zoning a city. You put the noisy factory away from the hospital and the school, you put the power station near the factories it serves. Board blocks work the same way.
A switching power supply is the factory, a precision measurement circuit is the hospital, and the traces are the roads.
The analogy breaks in one place: on a board every "road" also needs a clean return path beside it.
A floorplan for a mixed-signal board.
Noisy blocks (switcher, motor driver) are at one side, the digital core is in the middle, the analog and RF sections sit in their own corners, and the connectors line the bottom edge.
Note that nothing sensitive is adjacent to the switcher.
Functional partitioning: grouping circuits by role, such as power, digital, analog and RF ("When and why to separate grounds").
Noise source and victim: a block that gives off interference, and one that suffers from it.
Linear regulator: a simple supply that lowers a voltage by burning the difference as heat. Switching regulator (buck): a supply that lowers a voltage by switching rapidly.
It wastes little power but is electrically noisy. Thermal resistance: how many degrees a part heats up per watt it burns, in °C/W ("Reducing component heating on the board").
A linear regulator drops 5 volts to 3. 3 volts at 0. 5 amps. It burns (5 - 3. 3) times 0. 5 = 0. 85 watts.
With 60 degrees Celsius/W of thermal resistance it heats up about 51 degrees Celsius. A buck converter that is 90% efficient wastes only about 0.
18 watts, so in the same package it heats up about 11 degrees Celsius, but it makes electrical noise instead.
Either way the choice shapes the floorplan: keep the hot linear part away from a precision voltage reference that drifts with temperature, and keep the noisy buck away from sensitive inputs.
That is the whole idea.
"I floorplan before routing.

I start from the block diagram, mark noisy blocks (switching supplies, clocks, drivers), sensitive ones (ADC, reference, RF receive) and hot ones, and place connectors and mounting holes per the enclosure.

Then I let the signal flow run in a line through the board, keep noisy and sensitive blocks apart, put each supply close to its load, decoupling and crystals at their ICs, and keep the ground plane solid.
I check the ratsnest and thermals, then route."
